newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ research links milk protein to diabetes onset.
newsitem.headline: NZ research links milk protein to diabetes onset.

text.p: New Zealand's farm minister and its vital dairy industry moved quickly to control damage on Thursday after researchers said milk could trigger diabetes in people genetically predisposed to the disease.
New Zealand is the world's largest dairy exporter, with exports worth NZ$5 billion (US$3.47 billion) annually.

Research by professor Bob Elliott at Auckland Medical School linked the onset of insulin-dependent diabetes to milk containing a protein known as A1. About 80 percent of New Zealand's three-million-strong dairy herd have the gene that produces it.
Five percent of humans -- around 175,000 people in New Zealand -- are genetically vulnerable to insulin-dependent diabetes, but it develops in fewer than one percent of people.

"This is not the sort of thing that should cause any panic at all," Agriculture Minister Lockwood Smith said. "People have been drinking cow's milk, because it's a very healthy food, for years, for generations."
The New Zealand Dairy Board, which helped fund the research, said people should not avoid dairy products out of fear they might be predisposed to the disease.
"This research is not yet proven. It is vital people understand that is the case," said Dairy Research Institute director Kevin Marshall.

Marshall said the Dairy Board would act quickly if further research proved a link between A1 and diabetes. It could have A1-free milk on shop shelves within a year, but to suggest that should happen immediately was "scaremongering".

The health ministry said Elliott's research, which involved only animals and laboratory testing, was preliminary. It contained insufficient information for the ministry to make any public health recommendation.

Elliott, who presented a paper on his research to an international dairy conference in New Zealand, said experiments were needed to see if the diabetes rate went down when milk containing A1 protein was withdrawn.

Smith said the Dairy Board was isolating cows producing milk with the alternative A2 protein, and was applying for patents to commercially market milk products containing only A2, should this be necessary.

But Elliott said it would be difficult to provide people with dairy products free of A1. Demand would probably far outstrip supply for many years, until the nation's dairy herd was restocked with cows missing the gene that produced A1.

Elliott said even steering clear of milk would do little to help those predisposed to insulin-dependent diabetes because casein, or milk protein, was used in a wide variety of foods including ice cream, cheese and sausages. "It's virtually impossible to remove milk from the diet," he said.
Dairy Board public relations manager Neville Martin said sales could dip briefly on the back of the research but they should soon return to normal.
"Hopefully, the public will finally be shown...both sides of the balanced picture, and realise there is absolutely no reason whatsoever to run around and say the sky is falling."
